'''Stephen Francis Barker''' (January 11, 1927<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 24, 1963 |title=Reports of the President and of the Treasurer |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2o_WAAAAMAAJ&q=Stephen+Francis+Barker+January+11,+1927 |publisher=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |via=Google Books}}</ref> – December 16, 2019<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.everhere.com/us/obituaries/md/baltimore/stephen-barker-10132776|title=Stephen Barker Obituary (2019) &#124; Baltimore, Maryland|website=everhere.com}}</ref>)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hub.jhu.edu/2019/12/20/stephen-barker-649-em0-art1-dtd/|title=Longtime philosophy Professor Stephen Barker dies at 92|date=December 20, 2019|website=The Hub}}</ref> was an American [[philosophy of mathematics|philosopher of mathematics]], a [[professor emeritus]] of [[philosophy]] in the Department of Philosophy, [[Zanvyl Krieger School of Arts and Sciences|Krieger School of Arts and Sciences]] at  [[Johns Hopkins University]].<ref name=Wallach>{{Cite web |last=Wallach |first=Rachel |date=2019-12-20 |title=Longtime philosophy Professor Stephen Barker dies at 92 |url=https://hub.jhu.edu/2019/12/20/stephen-barker-649-em0-art1-dtd/ |access-date=2023-07-26 |website=The Hub |language=en}}</ref> He was also a faculty member at the [[University of Southern California]],<ref name="ReferenceA">"Dr. Barker Receives Harvard Fellowship," ''Daily Trojan'', Vol. 46, No. 136, May 16, 1955</ref> the [[University of Virginia]] and [[Ohio State University]].<ref name="profile">{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20121214220104/http://advanced.jhu.edu/faculty/view/?id=492|title=Faculty profile}}, JHU, retrieved 2011-06-10.</ref>

He was born in [[Ann Arbor]], [[Michigan]]. In 1948, he served in the [[United States Navy|Navy]] for a year. He then proceeded in 1949 to earn a  bachelor's degree from [[Swarthmore College]]. He got his master's degree as well as Ph.D in philosophy from Harvard University in 1951 and 1954 respectively.  While at Harvard, he won the [[Louise Seaman Bechtel#The Bechtel Prize|Bechtel Prize]] in 1951 for his essay, "A Study of Phenomenalism".<ref>{{citation |title=Eleven Awarded Annual Prizes From Essay Endowment Funds |date=June 7, 1951 |url=http://www.thecrimson.com/article/1951/6/7/eleven-awarded-annual-prizes-from-essay/ |journal=The Harvard Crimson}}.</ref><ref name=Wallach />

Later, he became an instructor in the [[University of Southern California]] in 1954–55. He became an [[assistant professor]] in the [[University of Virginia]] and then was made an [[associate professor]] in the same university from 1956 to 1961. He became a professor at [[Ohio State University]] from 1961 to1964. He reached the peak of his career when he arrived at Johns Hopkins as a professor in 1964 where he was named professor emeritus upon his retirement in 2002.<ref name=Wallach />

Barker was not just a professor or a professor emeritus, he was also a [https://worldwide.harvard.edu/frederick-sheldon-traveling-fellowships Sheldon Traveling Fellow] in England in 1952–53. Harvard awarded him the George Santayana Fellowship for the academic year 1955–56. In addition, he became a [[Guggenheim Fellow]] in 1964–65.<ref name=Wallach />

Barker was married to Evelyn Barker, who was also a philosopher and died in 2003. Baker himself eventually died in 2019 at 92 years of age.

== Books ==
Barker is the author of:
*''Induction and hypothesis: a study of the logic of confirmation'' (Cornell University Press, 1957). This study of theories of informal reasoning is structured in four parts: an investigation of the [[problem of induction]], a rejection of explanations based on overriding premises (such as the uniformity of nature) as a form of [[begging the question]], an overview of [[logical positivism|positivist]] approaches to the problem, and finally a resolution to the problem based on theories of [[John George Kemeny]] involving the selection of the most likely hypothesis to fit a set of observations.<ref>Review of ''Induction and hypothesis'' by [[Horace Romano Harré|R. Harré]] (1962), ''Mind''
(New Ser.) '''71''' (283): 412–420, {{JSTOR|2252092}}.</ref>
*''Philosophy of mathematics'' (Prentice-Hall, 1964). Part of a series of books (edited by Elizabeth and [[Monroe Beardsley]]) overviewing the main areas of philosophy, this book describes the main problems in the [[philosophy of mathematics]] and evaluates their proposed solutions. Its five chapters concern [[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean]] and [[non-Euclidean geometry]], and literalist and non-literalist views on the meaning of numbers.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Review | title = ''Philosophy of mathematics'' by Stanley J. Bezuszka (1964) | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume = 145 | issue = 3633| pages = 694–695 | doi = 10.1126/science.145.3633.694-a | s2cid = 170554292 }}</ref><ref>Review of ''Philosophy of mathematics'' by P. J. Davis, {{MR|0160705}}.</ref>
*''The elements of logic'' (McGraw Hill, 1965)
*''Thomas Reid  critical interpretations'' (with Tom L. Beauchamp, Philosophical monographs, 1976)

In addition, he edited [[John Wisdom]]'s ''Proof and explanation: the Virginia lectures'' (University Press of America, 1991), co-edited ''The Legacy of logical positivism; studies in the philosophy of science'' with [[Peter Achinstein]] (Johns Hopkins Press, 1969),<ref>[http://www.frame-poythress.org/frame_articles/1972Achinstein.htm Review] of ''The Legacy of logical positivism'' by John M. Frame, ''Westminster Theological Journal'' '''34''' (2): 199–201.</ref>
